Twenty-three out of twenty-four. That is how many times the S&P500 finished higher in this exact midterm window. The only loss began in nineteen thirty, the first full year of the Great Depression. On September twenty-seventh, twenty twenty-six, Observation Twenty-Five begins. War with Iran. Oil recently near ninety dollars. Inflation at three point four percent. Fear that artificial intelligence could replace millions of jobs. And President Trump's approval rating near thirty-three percent, with the midterm elections approaching. By the headlines, twenty twenty-six looks like a difficult time for stocks. Yet the historical record points the other way. That sounds bullish. But the real signal in twenty twenty-six may not be another win. It may be what happens if this pattern breaks. And the number I will be watching is minus twenty percent. If the market falls beyond that line, it will have traveled farther down than every previous winning cycle in this record. Then we would have to ask a much bigger question. Did a pattern fail, or did something in the market itself change? TradeWave is a historical analytics machine. It is a map of what happened in comparable periods. It cannot promise where we will end up, but it can show when the market has moved beyond every previous winning path. Here is the rule. The window runs from September twenty-seventh of a United States midterm-election year through July eighteenth of the following year, a total of two hundred ninety-five calendar days. Because both dates fall on Sunday this cycle, TradeWave records the next trading closes: Monday, September twenty-eighth, and Monday, July nineteenth, twenty twenty-seven. The dates are fixed before we know the result. No moving the goalposts later. When TradeWave first produced this chart, almost every bar was green. My first thought was not, I found something. My first thought was, Something must be wrong. I saved it, moved on, and opened it again about an hour later. Then I checked it again. Same result. These were not twenty-three years in a row. They were twenty-three separate midterm cycles spread across almost a century. Yet the same window finished higher twenty-three times out of twenty-four. That investigation eventually became my book, The One Hundred Year Pattern. The Stock Trader's Almanac had called the broader season the market's Sweet Spot. TradeWave let me narrow it to exact dates and see what happened inside every cycle back to nineteen thirty. And what happened inside those green bars changes the whole story. Across all twenty-four completed windows, the average return and the middle result were both about nineteen percent. But twenty-one of the twenty-three winners fell below their starting price before they finished higher. That is the part a simple green bar hides. TradeWave measures the best and worst point reached inside each window. Traders call them MFE and MAE. You do not need to remember the letters. The final return shows the destination. MFE and MAE show what happened on the road. In twenty eighteen, the market fell nineteen point five percent below its starting price. Then it recovered and finished up two point eight percent. The final bar is green. But that green bar hides a frightening decline. Then there is nineteen thirty. The worst point was more than thirty-five percent below the start. The window finally closed down twenty-three point four percent. So twenty-three green bars do not mean twenty-three easy rides. They give us three very different ways to read Observation Twenty-Five. First, the market could fall, perhaps sharply, then recover and finish higher. That would feel frightening. But it would still fit the old map. Most winners went underwater first. Second, the market could finish a little below its starting price. That would create the second red bar. It would weaken the record, but a pattern can fail once without the whole market changing. The third outcome is different. Remember the line from the beginning. Minus twenty percent. The deepest decline inside any previous winner was nineteen point five percent, in twenty eighteen. If the S&P500 falls more than roughly twenty percent below its September starting price, it will have moved beyond every previous winning path in this record. And if that decline stays deep and the window ends with a meaningful loss, I would treat it as evidence that the market may be playing by different rules. That would not prove another Great Depression had begun. But because the only major loss in this record began in nineteen thirty, I would take the possibility of a much darker market regime far more seriously. The failure itself would become information. Now consider the approaching midterms. Would the Trump administration try hard to support the economy and the market before voters go to the polls? An administration can affect taxes, spending, energy policy, regulation, and confidence. But it cannot order the market higher or control earnings, rates, oil, wars, and investors. That political effort is one more force inside the observation. It is not the answer to it. On Monday, September twenty-eighth, I will record the starting close. From that starting close, I will track the actual best point, the worst point, and the final close on July nineteenth, twenty twenty-seven. Will Observation Twenty-Five join
the wall of green bars? Will it suffer a frightening decline and recover, like twenty eighteen? Or will it cross the line no previous winner crossed, and possibly become the first meaningful break in this pattern since the Great Depression? We do not know. That is what makes this worth watching. The dates are fixed. The history is visible. And the twenty-fifth result has not been written yet. Subscribe, because I will track the complete journey through July, including the declines that a final green bar could hide. TradeWave shows us what happened. We interpret what it means. Now the market gets to write Observation Twenty-Five.
